title.text:
Automation 1: a
rule-based workflow

objects.text: What can a workflow of plain rules do for my messages, and where does it stop?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 6 of 12
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome. Today is a demonstration, and nobody builds anything. I show you an automation made only of plain rules, running on the same twelve customer messages you met in Session 1. The results are recorded in advance, so we spend our time on what they mean. First, three questions from Session 5.

The question for today is this: What can a workflow of plain rules do for my messages, and where does it stop? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

title.text:
Your two hours: mostly a
demonstration, then your own task

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_7e0ce6c2.png

objects.text: This is a demonstration: 15 of the 120 minutes are about your own task.

slides.notes:
Mostly I show and you watch. Twenty minutes for the four parts of an automation, then twenty-five for the router on the twelve messages. After the break I add a payment rule and show what it fixes and what it breaks, then ten minutes on the five controls.

The last twenty-five are yours: fifteen to write a rule and its five controls for your own task, then a short decision and the close.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  In the agreement review, what was the agreement compared with, and what did each flag need?
2.  Why is shortlisting CVs with AI a risk, and who decides?
3.  What did the meeting notes have to become before they were useful?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 5. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. In the agreement review, what was the agreement compared with, and what did each flag need? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. It was compared with the company’s own review playbook, which says what the company will and will not accept. Each flag needs a quote from the agreement so a person can check it.

Question two. Why is shortlisting CVs with AI a risk, and who decides? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. The AI gives fluent reasons that can hide bias, and it can slip on a detail such as a date count: run 1 counted two years for 2023 to present. A person decides, with the criteria written first.

Question three. What did the meeting notes have to become before they were useful? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. A list of decisions and actions, each with an owner and a date, checked against the notes.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Automation. A set of steps that runs by itself when something happens, with no person starting each run.

Trigger. The event that starts an automation, such as a new row of messages in a sheet.

Rule. A fixed test on the data, for example: the text contains the word late.

Route. Sending the message to a queue, which is the list one team works from.

Log. A record of each run: what came in, which rule fired and where it went.

title.text:
Every automation has four parts:
trigger, rules, route and log

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_11b0dc05.png
objects.alt: Every automation has four parts: trigger, rules, route and log

objects.text: If you can name these four parts for a task, you can judge a tool for it.

slides.notes:
Start with the plain idea. An automation does a job by itself when something happens. It has four parts. The trigger is the event that starts it, here a new message. The rules are fixed tests on the words. The route sends the message to the right queue, which is the list one team works from.

The log records what happened. Whatever the tool or the price, a vendor demonstration will show you these four parts. If you can name them for your own task, you can judge what you are being sold.

title.text:
The Session 1 rule drawn as a router:
one question, two queues and a log

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_rulechain_11.90x4.25_1e61eff0.png
objects.alt: The Session 1 rule drawn as a router: one question, two queues and a log

objects.text: The Session 1 rule with a route and a log. Non-complaints go to the Sales desk for now.

slides.notes:
Here is the keyword rule from Session 1 drawn as a workflow. A new row of messages is the trigger. One rule asks whether the text contains late or delay. If yes, the message goes to the Customer Service queue. If no rule fires, it goes to the Sales desk, which handles orders and everything else.

Every message leaves one row in the log. For now, anything that is not a complaint goes to the Sales desk, which is a simple choice I made for the demonstration. The picture has no AI in it. Each box is a fixed test or a fixed action, so you can predict every result in advance.

The same logic runs in a
spreadsheet or in a no-code tool

A new row of messages is pasted in

A formula: if the text contains late or delay
A filter or branch step with the same words
A column names the queue and people filter on it
A step sends the row to that queue’s sheet or inbox
Columns for the rule that fired and the queue
A step adds one row to a log sheet

slides.notes:
The same four parts can live in two places. In a spreadsheet, the rule is a formula, the route is a column, and anyone can see and edit it. In a no-code automation tool, Zapier is one example and there are others, the trigger is a new row or email and the rules are a filter or a branch step.

The tool then runs by itself, without anyone opening the sheet. I am describing the logic and not showing any screen, because step names and plans change. Check what a tool offers on its own page when you need it.

Now the demonstration. The results on the next slides are recorded: I computed them from the messages file and the answer key on the fourth of November 2026. The logic is two short formulas in a sheet, and I can show them if time allows, which is optional.

No AI ran, so every result is the same each time. Compare each queue with the key and ask two questions. Which messages went to the wrong queue?

title.text:
Used as a router, the complaint rule puts
5 of 12 messages in the right queue

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_verdicts_11.90x4.25_422cc217.png
objects.alt: Used as a router, the complaint rule puts 5 of 12 messages in the right queue

objects.text: Computed, not run. Session 1 counted only complaint or not: 7 of 12.

slides.notes:
Here is the router on the twelve messages. The right queue is the one the answer key implies: payments to Finance, complaints to Customer Service, orders and everything else to the Sales desk. Five of twelve land in the right queue. In Session 1 I asked only whether each message was a complaint, and the rule was right for seven.

The difference is the two payments, M02 and M14. The rule has no way to find a payment, so both go to the Sales desk. This result is computed from the files and is the same every time.

title.text: The 7 wrong routes come from three causes

rows.text: The word late sits in a normal order, so it goes to Customer Service.
Wet sugar, a polite note and a sarcastic thanks use neither word.
A payment with no payment rule
Both reach the Sales desk. Nothing looks for payment words yet.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_flag_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_speech_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.50.png

objects.text: On all 40 messages in the file, the rule flags only 2, both wrong, and finds none of the 9 complaints.

slides.notes:
Seven wrong routes, three causes. The first is a false alarm: M07 and M38 are normal orders that happen to contain the word late. The second is the complaint with no keyword: M03, M10 and M32 are complaints, but wet sugar, a polite note and a sarcastic thank you do not use our two words.

The third is a payment with no payment rule, M02 and M14. I also ran the rule on all forty messages in the file. It flags two, both wrong, and finds none of the nine complaints. Twelve messages were kind to it.

title.text:
The log shows which rule sent each
message, so a wrong route can be traced

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_11.90x4.25_82a4a845.png
objects.alt: The log shows which rule sent each message, so a wrong route can be traced

objects.text: The last column is added by the person who checks the log against the key.

slides.notes:
This is what the log looks like, with four of the twelve rows. For each message it records the rule that fired, the queue and, once a person has checked, whether the route was right. Look at M07. The log says late fired, so you see at once why a polite order reminder landed in Customer Service.

Without a log, a wrong route is only a customer who is annoyed three days later. A log does not stop the mistake, but it tells you where to look and how often it happens.

title.text:
A policy becomes a rule placed
first: payment words go to Finance

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_rulechain_11.90x4.25_7a76feb7.png
objects.alt: A policy becomes a rule placed first: payment words go to Finance

objects.text: The first rule that fires decides the route, so the order matters.

slides.notes:
Now a policy. The company says payments go to Finance first. A policy turns into a rule, and I put it above the others. If the text contains paid, payment or MoMo, the message goes to Finance and stops. Only if that rule does not fire does the late and delay rule run.

The order matters, because the first rule that fires decides the route. I chose those three words after reading the twelve messages, and that choice is a weakness I come back to. First, let me show you what it fixes.

title.text:
The payment rule lifts the router
from 5 to 7 of 12 in the right queue

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_versus_11.90x4.25_ebe9be43.png
objects.alt: The payment rule lifts the router from 5 to 7 of 12 in the right queue

objects.text: Computed on the twelve. Five wrong routes remain: M03, M07, M10, M32, M38.

slides.notes:
Here is the effect, computed on the twelve messages. Before the payment rule, five of twelve land in the right queue. After it, seven. The two that moved are M02, the customer who paid by MoMo and wants confirmation, and M14, who paid and was refused a delivery.

Both now reach Finance, which is where the key says they belong. The rest is unchanged. M07 and M38 are still false alarms, and M03, M10 and M32 are still missed. One rule fixed exactly the problem it was written for, and nothing else.

title.text: What the payment rule breaks and leaves open

rows.text: M14 and M26 each hold two topics. A rule picks one queue, so the second topic is lost.
I chose paid, payment and MoMo after reading the twelve, so 7 of 12 flatters the rule.
On all 40 messages it finds 6 of the 9 payments and sends none wrongly. M08, M13 and M30 are missed.
Adding invoice sends M06, M23 (invoice complaints) and M37 (a lost invoice book) to Finance: 3 wrong sends, no new payment.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Now what it breaks. First, a rule sends each message to one queue. M14 is a payment and a delivery complaint, and M26 is an order and a leak. The second topic is lost. Second, I picked the three words after reading these twelve messages, so seven of twelve flatters the rule.

On all forty messages it finds six of the nine payments and wrongly sends none, and it misses M08, M13 and M30. Third, more words do not always help. Adding the word invoice sends three messages wrongly to Finance, M06 and M23, which are invoice complaints, and M37, a lost invoice book, and it finds no new payment. A rule must be tested on messages it has not seen.

title.text:
Rules are exact and easy to
explain, and they stop at meaning

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.75.png

objects.text: What rules do well

runs.text: Easy to explain to an auditor
Reliable words, such as a payment reference

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_flag_0.75.png

objects.text: Where rules stop

runs.text: Meaning: M10 and M32 pass unseen

objects.text: Use rules where the words are reliable. Put a person where they are not.

slides.notes:
So what do rules do well?

They give the same answer every time, which makes them easy to test and easy to explain to an auditor, and they are cheap to run. They work best where the words are reliable, like a payment reference or an invoice number. Where do they stop?

They cannot read meaning, so the polite complaint and the sarcastic thank you pass unseen. They cannot hold two topics. And someone must keep the word lists up to date as customers change how they write. Use a rule where the words are reliable, and put a person where they are not.

title.text:
Five controls every automation
needs before you trust it

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_person_0.70.png

objects.text: An owner: one named person answers for it.

objects.text: An off switch: you know where it is and who may use it.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.70.png

objects.text: A log: every run leaves a row you can read.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.70.png

objects.text: A person for exceptions: someone reads what the rules cannot place.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.70.png

objects.text: A test before trust: run known cases and compare with the key.

slides.notes:
Whatever tool or vendor you use, ask for these five controls. An owner, one named person who answers for the automation. An off switch, and you know where it is and who may use it. A log, so every run leaves a row you can read. A person for exceptions, someone who reads what the rules cannot place.

And a test before trust: run known cases and compare the result with a key before any real message goes through. If a vendor cannot show you all five, the automation is not ready.

Write your task, your choice and the one rule you would start with.

slides.notes:
Time to decide. Take the task you chose in Session 1. Where does it sit?

A rule is enough, if the words are fixed and a wrong route is cheap. Rules plus a person, if the rules route and someone reads what they cannot place. Needs AI, if meaning matters, and that is next session. Or stays with a person, if a wrong route costs too much.

Say your choice and one reason aloud. Then write the single rule you would start with, even if you chose another option.
